hints: Identify the parent functional group first. The $\text{-OH}$ directly on the benzene ring makes this a phenol, so numbering starts at the $\text{-OH}$ carbon as C1.
walkthrough:
Spot the parent group**
You are looking at a benzene ring with $\text{-OH}$ attached directly, so this is a phenol. That means C1 is the carbon bearing the $\text{OH}$ group, and all other numbers are counted from there to give the lowest set of locants.

hints: Draw a vertical line of symmetry through the $\text{OH}$ and $\text{Cl}$ groups and check which ring carbons and which $\text{CH}_{3}$ groups mirror each other.
For $^{1}\text{H}$ NMR, count distinct proton sets separately: ring $\text{H}$, methyl $\text{H}$ and phenolic $\text{OH}$, remembering symmetry makes equivalent protons give one peak.
walkthrough:
Find the symmetry plane**
Place R with $\text{OH}$ on the left and $\text{Cl}$ on the right. There is a horizontal plane of symmetry through $\text{HO-C}$, $\text{C-Cl}$ and the ring centre. The top half mirrors the bottom half perfectly.

Count carbon environments**
The two $\text{C-CH}_{3}$ ring carbons are equivalent (1 environment). The two $\text{CH}_{3}$ carbons are equivalent (1 environment). The two $\text{CH}$ ring carbons ortho to $\text{OH}$ are equivalent (1 environment). Then $\text{C-OH}$ is unique and $\text{C-Cl}$ is unique. That is $3 + 2 = 5$ distinct carbon environments, so 5 peaks in $^{13}\text{C}$ NMR.

Count proton environments**
The two aromatic $\text{H}$ atoms are equivalent (1 peak). The six methyl $\text{H}$ atoms in the two equivalent $\text{CH}_{3}$ groups are equivalent (1 peak). The phenolic $\text{OH}$ proton is unique (1 peak). Total $= 3$ peaks in $^{1}\text{H}$ NMR in $\text{CDCl}_{3}$.

Final answer: carbon-13 NMR: 5 peaks
proton NMR: 3 peaks

hints: Think about which proton in a phenol is acidic and labile enough to exchange rapidly with a protic deuterated solvent.
walkthrough:
Identify the disappearing proton**
Only $\text{O-H}$ and $\text{N-H}$ protons exchange quickly with deuterium. Here the only candidate is the phenolic $\text{OH}$. Aromatic $\text{C-H}$ and alkyl $\text{C-H}$ protons do not exchange.
Deuterium ($^{2}\text{H}$) is invisible in $^{1}\text{H}$ NMR, so once $\text{Ar-OH}$ becomes $\text{Ar-OD}$, that peak vanishes, leaving one less peak.

Final answer: The phenolic $\text{OH}$ proton exchanges with $\text{D}_{2}\text{O}$ to give $\text{OD}$ and $\text{HOD}$: $\text{Ar-OH} + \text{D}_{2}\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{Ar-OD} + \text{HOD}$, so the $\text{OH}$ signal disappears from the $^{1}\text{H}$ NMR spectrum.

hints: Recall that phenols are acidic enough to react with $\text{Na}$ to give $\text{H}_{2}$ plus a phenoxide, but the ring substituents $\text{Cl}$ and $\text{CH}_{3}$ are unchanged.
Recall that phenols react with $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCl}$ to form a phenyl ethanoate ester by replacing the $\text{H}$ of $\text{OH}$ with $\text{COCH}_{3}$.
Think about how strongly the $\text{-OH}$ group activates the ring to electrophilic substitution and which ring positions are still free in R.
For $\text{Br}_{2}\text{(aq)}$, predict how many $\text{Br}$ atoms substitute at the activated ortho positions to $\text{OH}$ when meta positions are blocked by $\text{CH}_{3}$.
For benzenediazonium chloride, recall that coupling occurs at the activated position ortho or para to $\text{OH}$, and check which is available here.

Classify each change: loss of $\text{H}$ to $\text{H}_{2}$ involves oxidation, ester formation from $\text{-OH}$ plus $\text{-COCl}$ loses $\text{HCl}$, while ring $\text{H}$ replacement by $\text{Br}$ or $\text{-N=N-Ar}$ keeps the ring intact.
walkthrough:
Reaction with sodium, acid base behaviour**
Think of phenol as a weak acid. $\text{Na}$ removes the phenolic proton: $$2\text{Ar-OH} + 2\text{Na} \rightarrow 2\text{Ar-O}^{-}\text{Na}^{+} + \text{H}_{2}$$ Only the $\text{OH}$ becomes $\text{O}^{-}\text{Na}^{+}$. The $\text{Cl}$ and two $\text{CH}_{3}$ groups on the ring are untouched. Because sodium is oxidised from 0 to +1 and $\text{H}^{+}$ is reduced to $\text{H}_{2}$, this is redox.

Reaction with ethanoyl chloride, ester formation**
Acyl chlorides esterify phenols rapidly: $$\text{Ar-OH} + \text{CH}_{3}\text{COCl} \rightarrow \text{Ar-OCOCH}_{3} + \text{HCl}$$ Draw the same substituted ring but with $\text{-O-C(=O)-CH}_{3}$ in place of $\text{-OH}$. A small molecule $\text{HCl}$ is eliminated as the two larger fragments join, so this is condensation.

Why the ring is so reactive**
The lone pair on phenolic oxygen donates into the ring, strongly activating ortho and para positions to electrophiles. In R, para to $\text{OH}$ is blocked by $\text{Cl}$, and both meta positions are blocked by $\text{CH}_{3}$. That leaves exactly the two ortho positions (C2 and C6 relative to $\text{OH}$) free and highly reactive.

Bromination with bromine water**
With $\text{Br}_{2}\text{(aq)}$ no Lewis acid is needed. Both free ortho $\text{H}$ atoms are replaced: $$\text{Ar-H} + \text{Br}_{2} \rightarrow \text{Ar-Br} + \text{HBr}$$ applied twice. The product keeps $\text{OH}$, $\text{Cl}$ and two $\text{CH}_{3}$ groups, plus two new $\text{Br}$ atoms ortho to $\text{OH}$. This is electrophilic substitution.

Azo coupling with diazonium salt**
$\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{-N}^{+}\equiv\text{N}$ is a weak electrophile that only attacks strongly activated rings like phenoxide or phenol. It couples ortho to the $\text{OH}$ group (para is blocked by $\text{Cl}$), giving: $$\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{-N}_{2}^{+} + \text{Ar-H} \rightarrow \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{-N=N-Ar} + \text{H}^{+}$$ Draw $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{-N=N-}$ attached to the R ring ortho to $\text{OH}$. This forms a coloured azo dye and is also electrophilic substitution.

Final answer: With $\text{Na}$: sodium 4-chloro-3,5-dimethylphenoxide, $\text{Ar-O}^{-}\text{Na}^{+}$ ( $\text{OH}$ to $\text{ONa}$ ), redox.
With $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCl}$: 4-chloro-3,5-dimethylphenyl ethanoate, $\text{Ar-OCOCH}_{3}$ ( $\text{OH}$ to $\text{OCOCH}_{3}$ ), condensation (esterification).
With $\text{Br}_{2}\text{(aq)}$: 2,6-dibromo-4-chloro-3,5-dimethylphenol (both ortho $\text{H}$ to $\text{OH}$ replaced by $\text{Br}$), electrophilic substitution.
With $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{N}_{2}^{+}\text{Cl}^{-}$: azo compound $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{-N=N-Ar}$ where $\text{Ar}$ is 4-chloro-3,5-dimethyl-2-hydroxyphenyl (coupling ortho to $\text{OH}$), electrophilic substitution (azo coupling).
